item.title: Kinetic Energy and Speed of Neon and Argon Samples
item.stimulus:
A student prepares three gas samples in identical rigid 2.00 L containers. Each container holds 0.100 mol of a single monatomic gas. Assume ideal behavior. The molar masses are Ne = 20.18 g/mol and Ar = 39.95 g/mol.

Sample | Gas | Temperature (K)
1 | Ne | 250.
2 | Ne | 500.
3 | Ar | 500.
item.model_answer:
(a) The average kinetic energy of particles is proportional to the Kelvin temperature. KE(2)/KE(1) = T(2)/T(1) = 500. K / 250. K = 2.00. The Ne atoms in sample 2 have twice the average kinetic energy of those in sample 1.

(b) Samples 2 and 3 are both at 500. K, so the Ne atoms and Ar atoms have the same average kinetic energy. Setting ½m(Ne)v(Ne)² = ½m(Ar)v(Ar)² gives v(Ne)/v(Ar) = √(m(Ar)/m(Ne)) = √(39.95/20.18) = √1.980 = 1.41. The lighter Ne atoms move about 1.41 times as fast on average as the Ar atoms.

(c) Compared with sample 1, the distribution for sample 2 has its peak at a higher speed, and the peak is lower and the curve is broader (more spread out toward high speeds). The total area under each curve is the same because both samples contain the same number of atoms (0.100 mol).

(d) Both samples have the same volume and number of atoms, but the Ne atoms in sample 2 are at a higher temperature and so move faster on average. Faster atoms strike the container walls more often and hit with greater force, so the pressure in sample 2 is greater.
item.verification_python:
import math
T1=250.0;T2=500.0
ratio_ke=T2/T1
assert abs(ratio_ke-2.00)<1e-9
mNe=20.18;mAr=39.95
mr=mAr/mNe
assert abs(mr-1.980)<0.001
v=math.sqrt(mr)
assert abs(v-1.41)<0.005
assert abs(v-1.407)<0.001
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio of the average kinetic energy of the Ne atoms in sample 2 to the average kinetic energy of the Ne atoms in sample 1. Justify your calculation.

criteria.text: Ratio of average kinetic energies (sample 2 : sample 1) = 2.00, because average kinetic energy is proportional to Kelvin temperature.
criteria.evidence: Response states that average KE is proportional to Kelvin temperature and computes 500./250. = 2.00.
criteria.fix: Remember Kelvin temperature is directly proportional to average kinetic energy; divide the two Kelvin temperatures to get the KE ratio.

parts.prompt: Compare the average kinetic energy of the Ne atoms in sample 2 with that of the Ar atoms in sample 3, then use KE = ½mv² to calculate the ratio of the average speed of the Ne atoms to the average speed of the Ar atoms.

criteria.text: Claims the average kinetic energies are equal, justified by both samples being at the same temperature (500. K).
criteria.evidence: Response states equal average KE and cites the identical Kelvin temperature as the reason.
criteria.fix: When temperatures are equal, state that average kinetic energies are equal regardless of particle mass or identity.

criteria.evidence: Response sets ½m(Ne)v(Ne)² = ½m(Ar)v(Ar)², solves for v(Ne)/v(Ar) = √(m(Ar)/m(Ne)), and reports about 1.41.
criteria.fix: Set the two ½mv² expressions equal, solve for the speed ratio, and take the square root of the inverted mass ratio.

parts.prompt: Describe how the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of atomic speeds for sample 2 differs from that for sample 1. Address the position of the peak, the height of the peak, and the total area under the curve.

criteria.text: Sample 2 curve has its peak at a higher speed, a lower and broader peak, and the same total area as sample 1 (same number of atoms).
criteria.evidence: Response states all three: peak shifted to higher speed, peak lower with wider spread, and equal area because both samples contain 0.100 mol.
criteria.fix: For a hotter sample, describe the peak shifting right, flattening and broadening, with area unchanged because particle count is constant.

parts.prompt: The pressure in sample 2 is greater than the pressure in sample 1. Explain this difference in terms of the motion of the Ne atoms.

criteria.text: Atoms in sample 2 move faster on average, so they collide with the container walls more frequently and with greater force, producing greater pressure.
criteria.evidence: Response links higher temperature to greater average speed and states both more frequent wall collisions and more forceful collisions (same volume and moles).
criteria.fix: Explain pressure using collisions with walls: mention both collision frequency and collision force increasing with faster particle motion.

failed: rubric_points: Part (c), criterion c1 bundles three independently observable comparisons—peak position, peak height, and total area—into one point rather than awarding one specific element. It also requires a wider spread, although part (c) asks only about peak position, peak height, and total area; a complete answer to those requested comparisons could therefore lose the point.
first.solve_issues: Part (b) has a minor terminology issue: applying KE = ½mv² to average kinetic energy directly yields a root-mean-square speed ratio, not a mean-speed ratio, because ⟨v²⟩ is not equal to ⟨v⟩². However, both speed measures have the same mass and temperature scaling for Maxwell–Boltzmann gases, so the requested average-speed ratio is still unambiguously 1.41.
